qualityRationale: Classroom quasi-experiment with a reasonably large school sample (N=182) and a controlled test-format manipulation, though not randomized at the individual level.

title: Critical Period Effects in Second Language Learning: The Influence of Maturational State on the Acquisition of English as a Second Language
authors: Johnson, J. S., & Newport, E. L.
design: Cross-sectional correlational study relating age of arrival in the United States to performance on an untimed grammaticality judgment test of English morphosyntax among native Chinese/Korean speakers.
population: 46 native Chinese or Korean speakers who arrived in the United States between ages 3 and 39 and had lived there at least five years, tested at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
outcome: Grammaticality-judgment performance declined roughly linearly with age of arrival up to puberty, after which performance was low and highly variable; early arrivals were significantly superior to later arrivals in English proficiency, supporting a maturational (critical period) constraint on L2 acquisition.
limitations: Cross-sectional correlational design confounds age of arrival with length of residence and amount/type of input, and relies on a single grammaticality-judgment measure of proficiency rather than multiple linguistic domains.
qualityRationale: Influential, carefully controlled cross-sectional study with a standardized proficiency measure, but correlational (non-experimental) with a modest convenience sample.

title: Context of Learning and Second Language Fluency in French: Comparing Regular Classroom, Study Abroad, and Intensive Domestic Immersion Programs
authors: Freed, B. F., Segalowitz, N., & Dewey, D. P.
design: Quasi-experimental comparative study measuring oral fluency gains via pre/post oral proficiency interviews across three naturally occurring learning-context groups (at-home classroom instruction, intensive domestic immersion, and study abroad).
population: 28 university-level learners of French enrolled in one of three learning contexts: a regular at-home classroom, an intensive summer immersion program, or a study-abroad program.
outcome: The intensive immersion group showed significant gains in multiple fluency measures (total words spoken, longest turn length, speech rate, speech fluidity); the study-abroad group improved significantly only in speech fluidity; the at-home classroom group showed no significant fluency gains, indicating learning context moderates fluency development.
limitations: Very small, non-randomly assigned group sizes (learners self-selected their learning context) confound context with learner motivation/background, and the study examined only French oral fluency over one semester.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental multi-group comparison with standardized pre/post oral proficiency measures, but small non-randomized samples per context group.

title: Why Are You Learning a Second Language? Motivational Orientations and Self-Determination Theory
authors: Noels, K. A., Pelletier, L. G., Clément, R., & Vallerand, R. J.
design: Correlational questionnaire study testing a self-determination-theory model of L2 motivation via Pearson correlations among motivation subscales and hypothesized antecedents/consequences.
population: 159 English-L1 undergraduate students (mean age 22, 70% women) learning French as an L2 at a bilingual Canadian university.
outcome: Motivation subtypes formed the hypothesized self-determination continuum: amotivation correlated positively with anxiety and negatively with perceived competence, freedom of choice, and intention to continue L2 study, while more self-determined (identified/intrinsic) motivation showed the opposite, expected pattern.
limitations: Cross-sectional correlational design cannot establish causation; the authors explicitly note that longitudinal or experimental designs are needed to test the proposed causal sequence.
qualityRationale: Psychometrically careful correlational study with a moderate real-learner sample, but not experimental so causal claims are limited.

title: Do Language Learners Recognize Pragmatic Violations? Pragmatic Versus Grammatical Awareness in Instructed L2 Learning
design: Quasi-experimental comparative survey using a 20-scenario videotaped judgment task to compare instructed ESL and EFL learners' (and their teachers') relative awareness of grammatical versus pragmatic violations.
population: 543 instructed L2 English learners plus 53 of their teachers, drawn from ESL settings in the United States and EFL settings in Hungary (with a secondary EFL sample of 112 learners in Italy).
outcome: ESL learners and their teachers rated pragmatic errors as more serious than grammatical errors, whereas EFL learners and teachers showed the reverse pattern, indicating instructional/exposure context shapes learners' pragmatic versus grammatical awareness.
limitations: Cross-sectional judgment-task design measures awareness/perception rather than actual pragmatic production, and the ESL/EFL groups differ in more ways than instructional context (e.g., immersion exposure), confounding interpretation.
qualityRationale: Large, multi-site comparative study with a validated judgment instrument, though cross-sectional and correlational rather than a randomized intervention.

title: The Impact of Reading on Second Language Learning
design: Quasi-experimental field study (the Fiji 'Book Flood') comparing two extensive-reading treatments (Shared Book Experience / Sustained Silent Reading) against a control group using the standard audio-lingual curriculum, with pre/post/follow-up language testing over two years.
population: Over 500 Year 4 and Year 5 pupils across 12 rural Fiji primary schools (8 Book Flood schools, 4 control schools) learning English as a second language.
outcome: Book Flood groups showed significantly larger gains than controls on reading, listening comprehension, and structures within the first year, extending to writing and other measures by the second year, with reported effect sizes ranging from 0.76 to 1.18 across seven language tests.
limitations: Schools rather than individual pupils were the unit of assignment (non-random, matched-group design), and the intervention was implemented in a specific low-resource Pacific-Islands context that may limit generalizability.
qualityRationale: Large, multi-school quasi-experiment with matched control groups and multiple language outcome measures, though school-level (not random) assignment.

title: Evidence in Support of Written Corrective Feedback
design: Quasi-experimental study with four intact low-intermediate ESL classes assigned to three written-corrective-feedback conditions plus a no-feedback control, with pretest, immediate posttest, and two-month delayed posttest.
population: Low-intermediate international ESL learners at two private language schools in Auckland, New Zealand.
institution: Auckland University of Technology, New Zealand
outcome: Learners who received focused written corrective feedback on English articles outperformed the no-feedback control group on the immediate posttest, and this accuracy gain was retained two months later.
limitations: Intact classes rather than individually randomized participants were used, and only two article uses (referential indefinite "a", referential definite "the") were targeted, limiting generalization to other structures.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental classroom study with a genuine control group and delayed retention measure.

title: Evidence on the Effectiveness of Comprehensive Error Correction in Second Language Writing
authors: Van Beuningen, C. G., De Jong, N. H., & Kuiken, F.
design: Classroom quasi-experiment with direct and indirect comprehensive-corrective-feedback groups plus two control conditions (self-correction, practice-only), measuring accuracy in revision and in new writing 1 and 4 weeks later.
population: Secondary school students (mean age approximately 14) in multilingual classrooms in the Netherlands.
outcome: Both direct and indirect comprehensive corrective feedback improved written accuracy relative to the two control conditions, both during revision and in new writing up to four weeks later, without simplifying learners' writing; direct feedback benefited grammatical accuracy most and indirect feedback benefited non-grammatical accuracy most.
limitations: Intact classroom assignment rather than individual randomization limits causal certainty about individual-level effects.
qualityRationale: Large classroom quasi-experiment (N=268) with two control conditions and delayed measurement of transfer to new writing.

title: The Impact of Single Versus Multiple Recasts on L2 Learners' Implicit and Explicit Knowledge
authors: Hassanzadeh, M., Marefat, F., & Ramezani, A.
design: Quasi-experimental pretest/immediate-posttest/delayed-posttest study with three intact EFL classes assigned to single-recast, multiple-recast, or control conditions over a two-month period.
population: Farsi-speaking adult (ages 17-40) lower-intermediate EFL learners at a language institute in Kerman, Iran.
outcome: Both single- and multiple-recast groups improved significantly over the control group on timed/untimed grammaticality-judgment and oral-imitation tasks (targeting English unreal conditionals) at immediate and delayed posttests; multiple recasts showed an added advantage on delayed oral imitation.
limitations: Authors note practical constraints administering the oral-imitation task outside a controlled lab, possible practice/test effects in the control group, and contamination from learners' concurrent regular coursework.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental classroom design with control group, multiple outcome measures, and delayed posttest, though limitations are self-acknowledged.

title: Implicit and Explicit Second Language Training Recruit Common Neural Mechanisms for Syntactic Processing
design: Laboratory experiment assigning adult native-English-speaking learners to implicit (meaning-focused exposure) or explicit (rule-instruction) training in an artificial French-based grammar, with behavioral grammaticality-judgment and ERP measures.
population: Native English-speaking adults (mean age approximately 21.6) with no prior fluency in a Romance language, tested at a US university laboratory.
outcome: Explicitly trained learners reached 89% grammaticality-judgment accuracy (d'=3.0) versus 64% (d'=0.94) for implicitly trained learners, but ERP P600 effects were predicted by proficiency level rather than training type, indicating both training routes can lead toward native-like syntactic processing.
limitations: The paradigm used a brief single-session artificial-language design with only two syntactic violation types, so findings may not generalize to naturalistic multi-day L2 classroom instruction.
qualityRationale: Randomized lab training study with behavioral and neural outcome measures; artificial-language paradigm limits ecological generalization.

title: Explicit and Implicit Second Language Training Differentially Affect the Achievement of Native-like Brain Activation Patterns
authors: Morgan-Short, K., Steinhauer, K., Sanz, C., & Ullman, M. T.
design: Randomized laboratory experiment assigning adult native English speakers to explicit (rule-plus-examples) or implicit (examples-only) training on an artificial language (Brocanto2), with longitudinal ERP testing at low and high proficiency.
population: Right-handed native-English-speaking adults (mean age approximately 24) with minimal prior Romance-language exposure.
outcome: Behavioral (d') scores did not differ significantly between explicit and implicit training groups at either proficiency level, but the two groups showed different ERP signatures at high proficiency (explicit: anterior positivity plus P600; implicit: N400 giving way to anterior negativity plus P600), with both trajectories converging toward native-like P600 patterns.
limitations: Results are limited to a small set of well-studied syntactic violation types in an artificial miniature language, so generalization to natural-language classroom learning is unconfirmed.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled lab training study with longitudinal behavioral and ERP measures; artificial-language paradigm limits ecological generalization.

title: Mobile-Assisted Focus on Forms in English for Academic Purposes Instruction: Investigating the Impacts on Learning Academic Words
design: Quasi-experimental (self-selected, non-random) pretest/posttest study comparing digital-flashcard (Anki app) review versus paper-based word-list review of Academic Word List items over a 3-month EAP course.
population: Adult Iranian EFL learners (mean age approximately 21) at intermediate CEFR proficiency in Tehran, Iran.
outcome: The digital-flashcard group significantly outperformed the word-list control group on receptive (p<=.005, partial eta-squared=0.20), productive (p<=.019, partial eta-squared=0.148), and contextual fill-in-the-blank (p<=.032, partial eta-squared=0.125) academic-vocabulary posttests.
limitations: Small sample size, non-random convenience/self-selected group assignment, and absence of a delayed posttest are explicitly acknowledged by the authors.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental classroom study with quantified effect sizes; self-selected (non-random) group assignment is an explicit author-acknowledged limitation.

title: How Do EFL Learners Process Oral Tasks With Different Complexity: An Exploratory Study
design: Repeated-measures, within-subject experiment in which learners performed two narrative tasks (simple vs. complex, manipulated by number of story elements) in counterbalanced order two weeks apart, with stimulated recall used to probe cognitive processing at each stage of speech production.
population: First-year Chinese non-English-major university students, native Mandarin speakers, EFL learners with 9+ years of English study and no residence in an English-speaking country, studying at Qufu Normal University, China.
institution: College of Foreign Languages, Qufu Normal University, China
outcome: Complex narrative tasks were associated with a smaller share of pre-articulation form-processing activity (~48% vs. ~55% for simple tasks) and roughly double the post-articulation form-monitoring activity (~20% vs. ~10%), though a chi-square test found no statistically significant overall difference in cognitive-activity distribution across task complexity (chi-square=1.951, p=0.377).
limitations: Very small sample (N=10) from a single institution and no control group beyond within-subject comparison, and the study relied on stimulated recall, which may not fully capture real-time cognitive processing.
qualityRationale: Real controlled within-subject experiment with a clear task-complexity manipulation, but very small single-site sample limits statistical power and generalizability.

title: Effects of Distributed Practice on the Acquisition of Second Language English Syntax
design: Quasi-experiment manipulating intersession interval (3-day vs. 14-day gaps between two practice sessions on English grammar tasks) crossed with retention interval (7-day vs. 60-day delayed post-test).
population: First-year university students (ages 19-23) enrolled in an economics and business degree program, L1 Malay, intermediate English proficiency, in the United Arab Emirates.
outcome: At the 7-day retention test, the 3-day and 14-day intersession-interval groups did not differ significantly on either grammar task; at the 60-day retention test, the 14-day (distributed) group significantly outperformed the 3-day (massed) group on both tasks, supporting a spacing effect for L2 grammar learning that emerges over longer retention intervals.
limitations: Single L1 (Malay) and single institutional population limits generalizability; the published article required a subsequent erratum correcting a repeated spelling error, though this does not affect the reported statistics.
qualityRationale: Controlled quasi-experimental design manipulating two independent spacing variables with delayed retention tests, from a single-institution intermediate-proficiency sample.

title: Computer Assisted Pronunciation Training: Targeting Second Language Vowel Perception Improves Pronunciation
design: Pre-test/post-test training study using a custom computer application presenting high-variability recordings of ten Canadian English vowels (produced by twenty native speakers) in monosyllabic frames, with intelligibility assessed in trained and untrained contexts.
population: Adult Mandarin-speaking learners of English as a second language.
outcome: Vowel intelligibility significantly improved as a result of high-variability perceptual training, and the gains transferred to an untrained production context, though improvement did not extend to a third, more distant tested context.
limitations: Small sample (N=22) with no untreated control group described in the available abstract, and transfer of training gains was incomplete (did not reach the third test context).
qualityRationale: Controlled pre/post training study with a validated high-variability phonetic training paradigm and multi-context transfer testing, on a modest single-L1 sample.

title: Effects of Practice Variability on Second-Language Speech Production Training
authors: Bu, L., Nagano, M., Harel, D., & McAllister, T.
design: Single-subject experimental design with multiple baselines across behaviors; participants were randomly assigned to high-variability or low-variability speech-production practice conditions targeting English rhotics, with acoustic (F1/F2/F3) measures taken pre-, post-, and at maintenance.
population: Adult native Korean speakers (ages 25-43, mean 30.9), residing in the U.S. for two years or less, with 3-25 years of prior English instruction (mean 11.5 years).
institution: New York University, Department of Communicative Sciences and Disorders
outcome: High-variability practice produced a significant short-term change in F3-F2 distance for the target /r/ sound (p<0.001) relative to low-variability practice, but long-term maintenance gains were limited, with only one of eight participants reaching a functionally relevant effect size at follow-up (effect sizes ranged from d=-1.26 to 0.29 across participants).
limitations: Very small, heterogeneous single-site sample with unequal gender distribution across conditions, acoustic rather than listener-perceptual outcome measures, and no control condition for the tactile feedback device used in training.
qualityRationale: Rigorous single-subject experimental design with randomized condition assignment and objective acoustic measures, but N=8 and limited long-term maintenance evidence.

title: Awareness, Different Learning Conditions, and Second Language Development
authors: Rosa, E. M., & Leow, R. P.
design: Quasi-experimental study using a computerized problem-solving task with concurrent/retrospective verbal reports, comparing learners exposed to versions of the task varying in explicitness regarding the Spanish past conditional.
population: Adult L2 learners of Spanish enrolled at a US university.
topic: focused L2 instruction and form-focused instruction
outcome: Learners who reached higher levels of awareness (understanding) under more explicit task conditions showed significantly greater gains on recognition and production of the target Spanish past-conditional forms than learners with lower awareness.
limitations: Awareness was measured via concurrent/retrospective verbal report protocols, which risk reactivity that can itself alter the cognitive process being measured.
qualityRationale: Controlled quasi-experimental lab/classroom study with verbal-report measures rather than a large-scale randomized trial.

title: Willingness to Communicate in a Second Language: The Japanese EFL Context
design: Cross-sectional correlational survey study testing a hypothesized structural equation model linking L2 learning and communication variables.
population: Japanese university students learning English as a foreign language.
outcome: International posture predicted motivation, which predicted L2 proficiency and communication confidence, which in turn predicted willingness to communicate in English; the hypothesized structural model fit the data well.
limitations: Cross-sectional self-report survey design cannot establish causal direction between motivation, confidence, and willingness to communicate.
qualityRationale: Large-sample correlational SEM survey study; controlled measurement model but not an experimental design.

title: The L2 Motivational Self System, L2 Anxiety, and Motivated Behavior: A Structural Equation Modeling Approach
design: Cross-sectional correlational survey study using structural equation modeling.
population: Iranian high school students learning English as a foreign language.
institution: Iran University of Science and Technology
outcome: The ideal L2 self and L2 learning experience were associated with lower L2 anxiety and greater motivated learning behavior, while the ought-to L2 self was associated with higher anxiety.
limitations: Relies entirely on self-report questionnaire data from a single national/educational context, limiting generalizability and precluding causal inference.
qualityRationale: Large-sample correlational SEM survey study; controlled measurement model but not an experimental design.

title: The Effects of Guided Careful Online Planning on Complexity, Accuracy and Fluency in Intermediate EFL Learners' Oral Production: The Case of English Articles
design: Experimental study with three between-subjects planning conditions (guided careful online planning, unguided careful online planning, pressured online planning) on an oral narrative task.
population: Intermediate Iranian EFL learners.
outcome: Guided careful online planning produced significantly more accurate use of English articles and greater grammatical complexity than pressured planning, but at a measurable cost to speech fluency relative to unguided/pressured planners.
limitations: Small single-task, single-structure (English articles) design limits generalization to other grammatical forms or task types.
qualityRationale: Controlled classroom experiment with random assignment to planning conditions but a modest single-site sample.

title: The Effects of Pre-Task Planning and On-Line Planning on Fluency, Complexity and Accuracy in L2 Monologic Oral Production
design: Experimental study comparing no-planning, pre-task-planning, and unpressured online-planning conditions on an oral narrative task.
population: Chinese EFL learners at a university in China.
outcome: Pre-task planning increased fluency and grammatical complexity, while unpressured online planning increased accuracy and grammatical complexity, showing planning type has differential effects on the components of oral production.
limitations: Small sample split across three groups (14 per group) performing a single narrative task type, limiting statistical power and task-type generalizability.
qualityRationale: Controlled experimental task-based study with random assignment to planning conditions but a modest sample per cell.

title: Processing Instruction and Meaningful Output-Based Instruction: Effects on Second Language Development
design: Experimental study with three between-subjects conditions (processing instruction, meaningful output-based instruction, control) on comprehension and production of a Spanish grammatical structure.
population: First-semester university learners of Spanish.
outcome: Both processing instruction and meaningful output-based instruction produced significant gains over the control on interpretation and production tasks, but only the output-based group showed significantly greater gains on production measures.
limitations: Single grammatical target and single proficiency level (first-semester learners) limits generalization to other structures or more advanced learners.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled classroom experiment with a clearly reported sample size and design, though limited to one structure and one proficiency level.

title: The Role of Learning Environment in the Development of Pragmatic Comprehension: A Comparison of Gains Between EFL and ESL Learners
design: Quasi-experimental longitudinal comparison of pragmatic comprehension development (accuracy and response-time speed) using a computerized listening instrument, administered before and after roughly 120-130 hours of instruction.
population: 60 Japanese EFL learners in Japan and 57 ESL learners in the United States.
outcome: Both groups improved significantly in comprehension of indirect refusals/opinions, but EFL learners gained mainly in accuracy while ESL learners gained mainly in comprehension speed, showing learning environment shapes which dimension of pragmatic comprehension develops.
limitations: EFL and ESL groups were not randomly assigned and differed in more than just learning environment (e.g., institutional context, amount of daily English exposure), confounding the environment comparison.
qualityRationale: Controlled longitudinal quasi-experimental comparison with a reasonably sized cross-national sample, but non-random group assignment.

title: The Effects of Instruction on Learners' Production of Appropriate and Accurate Suggestions
design: Quasi-experimental study comparing explicit pragmatic instruction, implicit instruction (input enhancement plus recasts), and a control group across a 16-week semester.
population: Spanish learners of English enrolled in a university computer science course.
outcome: The explicit instruction group outperformed the implicit and control groups in producing appropriate and accurate head acts and downgraders in suggestion speech acts, indicating an advantage for explicit metapragmatic instruction over incidental exposure alone.
limitations: Instruction was embedded in intact, non-randomly-assigned class sections, and pragmatic production was assessed via a written discourse completion task rather than spontaneous spoken interaction.
qualityRationale: Controlled quasi-experimental classroom study with intact sections rather than individual random assignment.

title: Incidental Vocabulary Learning by Advanced Foreign Language Students: The Influence of Marginal Glosses, Dictionary Use, and Reoccurrence of Unknown Words
authors: Hulstijn, J. H., Hollander, M., & Greidanus, T.
design: Experimental study with three between-subjects reading conditions (marginal glosses, dictionary access, control) testing incidental vocabulary recall after reading a short story.
population: Advanced Dutch (L1) learners of French as a foreign language.
outcome: Frequency of word occurrence combined with access to meaning (via marginal glosses or dictionary use) produced greater incidental vocabulary learning than frequency of occurrence alone with no meaning support.
limitations: Vocabulary retention was tested with a single short narrative text and a fixed set of 16 target words, limiting generalization to other text types or larger vocabularies.
qualityRationale: Controlled experimental reading study with random assignment to gloss/dictionary/control conditions.

title: The Effects of Extensive Reading on Reading Comprehension, Reading Rate, and Vocabulary Acquisition
design: Quasi-experimental study using four intact classes (two control, two experimental) over a 15-week semester comparing an extensive-reading-plus-intensive-reading condition to an intensive-reading-only condition.
population: Korean university students learning English as a foreign language (88 control, 83 experimental).
institution: Pukyong National University, Busan, South Korea
outcome: The extensive reading group significantly outperformed the intensive-reading-only control group on the combined measure of reading comprehension, reading rate, and vocabulary acquisition.
limitations: Use of intact pre-existing classes rather than individual random assignment introduces a risk of pre-existing group differences confounding the treatment effect.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental classroom study with a reasonably large combined sample but non-random, intact-class assignment.

title: How Does Prior Word Knowledge Affect Vocabulary Learning Progress in an Extensive Reading Program?
design: Quasi-experimental longitudinal study tracking vocabulary gains from two sets of target words via pretests, immediate posttests, and a three-month delayed posttest across a 37-week extensive reading program.
population: EFL learners divided into high-, intermediate-, and low-proficiency groups reading graded readers.
outcome: Prior vocabulary knowledge strongly predicted vocabulary gains from extensive reading: relative gains were 63.18% for the high-level group versus 44.64% (intermediate) and 28.12% (low-level), with gains largely retained at the three-month follow-up.
limitations: Proficiency groups were not randomly assigned and differed systematically in starting vocabulary knowledge, which is itself the variable being studied, limiting causal claims about instructional design.
qualityRationale: Longitudinal quasi-experimental extensive-reading program study with delayed retention testing but non-random proficiency grouping.

title: Reexamining Effects of Form-Focused Instruction on L2 Pronunciation Development: The Role of Explicit Phonetic Information
design: Three-group (control, FFI-only, FFI plus explicit phonetic information) classroom experiment testing whether explicit phonetic information added to form-focused instruction improves L2 pronunciation of English /r/ by Japanese EFL learners, with generalization tests to unfamiliar words.
population: Japanese learners of English in an EFL setting, assigned to a control group (n=14), an FFI-only group (n=18), and an FFI plus explicit-phonetic-information group (n=17).
outcome: The FFI-only group showed moderate pronunciation improvement mainly in familiar contexts, while the FFI plus explicit-phonetic-information group showed considerably larger gains that generalized to unfamiliar lexical contexts beyond the instructional materials.
limitations: Group sizes were small (14-18 learners per condition) and all participants were Japanese EFL learners targeting a single phone (English /r/), limiting generalization to other L1 backgrounds or sounds.
qualityRationale: Controlled three-group classroom experiment with generalization testing, but small per-group samples and a single L1/single-phone population.

title: Acquiring Vocabulary through Reading: Effects of Frequency and Contextual Richness
authors: Zahar, R., Cobb, T., & Spada, N.
design: Pretest-posttest study measuring how word frequency of occurrence and contextual richness during reading of a graded text predicted vocabulary gains, compared across five ESL proficiency groups.
population: 144 male grade seven ESL students at a private Montreal French-language high school, placed into five proficiency streams (beginner to bilingual), with about 1.5 years of prior ESL instruction.
institution: McGill University; Université du Québec à Montréal; OISE/University of Toronto
outcome: Participants learned an average of 2.16 of the 30 target words tested from reading a graded text. Frequency of word occurrence needed for learning correlated with learner proficiency level (lower-proficiency learners needed more encounters), while contextual richness was unrelated to learning.
limitations: Single graded reading text and a narrow population (grade-7 male ESL students at one school) limit generalizability.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental single-cohort pretest-posttest design without a no-treatment control condition.

title: Vocabulary Acquisition from Extensive Reading: A Case Study
design: Single-participant case study tracking one learner of French through a one-month extensive reading program, using one-on-one interviews to measure gains in spelling, meaning, and grammatical knowledge for 133 target words, related to encounter frequency.
population: One adult learner of French as a foreign language, assessed via one-on-one interview before and after one month of extensive reading.
outcome: Knowledge of 65% of the 133 target words was enhanced in some way. Spelling was strongly enhanced even from a small number of exposures; meaning and grammatical knowledge were also enhanced, but less so.
limitations: Single-participant case-study design (N=1); findings cannot be generalized beyond this one learner and this one reading program.
qualityRationale: Detailed single-case design with strong measurement, but N=1 means no between-subjects control and limited generalizability.

title: Learning L2 Vocabulary through Extensive Reading: A Measurement Study
design: Pilot measurement study within an extensive reading program, using electronic scanning, lexical frequency profiling, and individualized checklist testing to identify which words learners encountered and measure the proportion actually learned.
population: 21 ESL learners who freely chose their own reading books within a pilot extensive reading program.
outcome: The new measurement methodology (electronic scanning plus individualized checklist testing) proved feasible and effective for assessing word-knowledge gains; observed vocabulary growth rates were higher than those found in earlier studies.
limitations: Small pilot sample (n=21) with self-selected reading material and no untreated control group.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experimental pilot (single group, no control condition) focused on validating a measurement method rather than a controlled comparison.

title: A Comparison of the Effects of Reading and Listening on Incidental Vocabulary Acquisition
design: Between-subjects experiment comparing incidental vocabulary acquisition from reading academic texts versus listening to academic lectures (plus a no-input control), assessed immediately and after a delay, across four learner proficiency levels.
population: 230 university-level EFL students in an English for Specific Purposes course, assigned to read three academic texts, listen to three academic lectures, or receive no input.
outcome: Reading subjects made greater vocabulary gains than listening subjects at all four proficiency levels analyzed; the reading advantage diminished at higher proficiency, and on a delayed posttest the highest-proficiency learners showed no significant difference between modes.
limitations: Input modes differed in more than text/speech (e.g., text type, exposure conditions), and only one delayed retention interval was tested.
qualityRationale: Large sample (N=230), between-subjects design with a no-input control condition and delayed posttest across multiple proficiency levels.

title: The Effects of Listening Support on the Listening Performance of EFL Learners
design: Classroom-based experiment comparing four types of listening support (question preview, input repetition, topic background knowledge, and vocabulary instruction) against a no-support condition on an L2 listening comprehension test.
population: 160 students enrolled in a required English listening course at a college in Taiwan.
institution: Hsing Wu College, Taiwan; University of Auckland
outcome: Providing background knowledge about the topic produced the greatest improvement in listening performance, followed by input repetition; vocabulary instruction was the least effective of the four supports, and proficiency level significantly moderated the effect of question preview.
limitations: Single institutional context (one Taiwanese college) with a fixed test format; the four support types were not fully crossed factorially.
qualityRationale: Reasonably large classroom sample (N=160) with a controlled comparison of four distinct support conditions against listening outcomes.

title: Motivation, Self-Confidence, and Group Cohesion in the Foreign Language Classroom
authors: Clément, R., Dörnyei, Z., & Noels, K. A.
design: Cross-sectional questionnaire study of attitudes, motivation, anxiety, self-confidence and classroom atmosphere/cohesion, analyzed with factor and correlational analyses to model relations between motivational orientations, self-confidence and achievement.
population: 301 Hungarian Grade 11 high school students learning English as a Foreign Language in the Budapest region.
outcome: Xenophilic, sociocultural, instrumental and media-use reasons were the most strongly endorsed motivational orientations; while all motivational subprocesses were associated with achievement, self-confidence and anxiety showed no relationship to classroom atmosphere.
limitations: Cross-sectional, single-context self-report questionnaire design limits causal inference and generalizability to other learning contexts.
qualityRationale: Large, well-known correlational survey with factor analysis but non-experimental, self-report, single cultural context.

title: Toward a Better Understanding of Language Learning Motivation in a Study Abroad Context: An Investigation Among Chinese English as a Foreign Language Learners
authors: Yue, Z., Zhao, K., Meng, Y., Qian, X., & Wu, L.
design: Mixed-methods study combining a questionnaire and semi-structured interviews with structural equation modeling to test relations among L2 self-concept, international posture, attitudes and motivated learning behavior/willingness to communicate.
population: 217 Chinese postgraduate students aged 22-23 pursuing master's degrees in the United Kingdom (EFL learners in a study-abroad context); 9 also interviewed.
institution: College of Teacher Education, Hebei Normal University
outcome: International posture was the strongest positive predictor of L2 learning effort/willingness to communicate, followed by the ideal L2 self; the ought-to L2 self had a significant negative impact, while attitudes toward the L2 community showed no evident role.
limitations: Authors state the small sample may not be representative of Chinese overseas students in general and the design lacked longitudinal data.
qualityRationale: Well-powered mixed-methods survey with SEM, but correlational/self-report and author-acknowledged sample representativeness limits.

title: Comparison of Foreign Language Anxiety Based on Four Language Skills in Chinese College Students
authors: Ran, C., Wang, Y., & Zhu, W.
design: Cross-sectional survey using four skill-specific Foreign Language Anxiety scales (speaking, listening, writing, reading), analyzed with descriptive statistics and independent-sample t-tests to compare anxiety levels and correlates across skills and gender.
population: First-year Chinese medical university students (284 male, 739 female, mean age ~18.3) who had studied English for at least 6 years in a regular classroom setting.
institution: China Medical University, Shenyang, Liaoning, China
outcome: Listening anxiety was the predominant form of foreign language anxiety (mean 106.863) while reading anxiety was lowest (mean 62.726); prior achievement and self-evaluation correlated negatively with anxiety on several skills.
limitations: Authors caution about generalizability given the restricted/volunteer sample, and note foreign language anxiety is a dynamic phenomenon requiring longitudinal follow-up.
qualityRationale: Large cross-sectional sample with validated scales, but non-random volunteer recruitment and correlational design limit causal claims.

title: Context, Contact, and Cognition in Oral Fluency Acquisition: Learning Spanish in At Home and Study Abroad Contexts
design: Quasi-experimental comparison of L2 oral fluency/proficiency gains (via Oral Proficiency Interview and temporal/hesitation measures) plus cognitive measures (lexical access speed, attention control) between two naturally occurring learning contexts over one semester.
population: 40 native English-speaking university students studying Spanish for one semester, in either an at-home classroom context or a study-abroad context.
outcome: Study-abroad learners showed greater gains on some oral fluency/proficiency measures than at-home learners, but outcomes reflected complex interactions among cognitive abilities, language contact and context rather than context alone.
limitations: Small, non-randomized sample with self-reported language-contact hours and only one target-language/context pairing.
qualityRationale: Naturalistic quasi-experimental comparison of learning contexts, not randomized, with modest sample size.

title: Age of Onset and Nativelikeness in a Second Language: Listener Perception Versus Linguistic Scrutiny
design: Two-phase study: native-speaker listener judgments of nativelikeness across a wide range of L2 age-of-onset, followed by detailed linguistic testing (10 tasks) of the subset judged passably native, comparing perceptual versus fine-grained measures of ultimate attainment.
population: 195 Spanish-L1/Swedish-L2 bilinguals with age of onset ranging from under 1 to 47 years, all self-identified as potentially nativelike; a subset of 41 was scrutinized in detail.
institution: Centre for Research on Bilingualism, Stockholm University
outcome: Only a small minority who began L2 acquisition after age 12 were perceived as native by listener judges, and under detailed linguistic scrutiny none of the late learners performed within the native-speaker range on all measures, while only some early learners did.
limitations: Relies on self-selected participants who believed they could pass as native speakers, and detailed scrutiny was only applied to the subset who passed initial perception judging.
qualityRationale: Large, carefully designed two-phase study combining perceptual and rigorous linguistic testing across a wide age-of-onset range.

title: The Age Factor Revisited: Timing in Acquisition Interacts With Age of Onset in Bilingual Acquisition
design: Longitudinal comparison (two test points 16 months apart) using a standardized morphosyntax/semantics test to compare early-L2 and simultaneous bilingual children against monolinguals on early- versus late-acquired grammatical phenomena.
population: 111 bilingual children and 49 monolingual children acquiring German, aged between about 4;4 and 5;8 years.
outcome: Simultaneous bilingual children had an early advantage over early-L2 peers on early-acquired grammatical phenomena that disappeared over time, while performance did not differ on late-acquired phenomena; home language dominance did not affect simultaneous bilinguals' performance.
limitations: Authors state they could not fully dissociate age-of-onset effects from length-of-exposure effects and measured dominance via questionnaire rather than fine-grained measures.
qualityRationale: Longitudinal design with standardized testing is a strength, but non-randomized naturalistic groups and an acknowledged confound between age of onset and length of exposure.

title: Learning Vocabulary Through Assisted Repeated Reading: How Much Time Should There Be Between Repetitions of the Same Text?
design: Classroom quasi-experiment comparing intensive (once daily for 5 consecutive days) versus spaced (once weekly for 5 consecutive weeks) assisted repeated reading of the same text, measuring vocabulary gains at immediate and delayed posttests.
population: 16-year-old learners of English as a foreign language in Taiwan.
outcome: Intensive practice led to more immediate vocabulary gains, but spaced practice led to greater long-term retention.
limitations: Single L1/context (Taiwanese EFL teenagers) and a single text/vocabulary set constrain generalizability.
qualityRationale: Classroom-based quasi-experimental comparison of two spacing schedules using intact groups rather than individual random assignment.

title: Spaced Vocabulary Acquisition While Incidental Listening by ESL University Students
authors: Zubenko, T., Gavrylenko, A., Zhyvotovska, T., & Vasylieva, N.
design: Quasi-experiment assigning learners to one experimental (spaced vocabulary acquisition strategy via 7 audio lessons) and two comparison groups, measuring incidental acquisition/retention of 120 English target words via an end-of-experiment test.
population: Second-year Ukrainian university students majoring in English as a second language, age 17-19.
institution: Petro Mohyla Black Sea National University, Mykolaiv, Ukraine
outcome: Students who used the spaced L2 vocabulary acquisition strategy outperformed the comparison group on the end-of-experiment test (84.1 versus 80.6).
limitations: Small, single-institution sample (N=51) across only three intact groups without described individual random assignment.
qualityRationale: Three-group comparison without described individual random assignment; small single-site sample.

title: Predicting Grades From an English Language Assessment: The Importance of Peeling the Onion
authors: Bridgeman, B., Cho, Y., & DiPietro, S.
design: Correlational predictive-validity study relating TOEFL iBT scores to first-year GPA, comparing a single pooled analysis against analyses disaggregated by discipline and nationality subgroup.
population: 787 international undergraduate students at an urban U.S. university, including subsamples of Chinese engineering and business majors.
outcome: When all students were pooled, the correlation of TOEFL scores with GPA was 0.18; in a subsample of engineering students from China the correlation was 0.58 (0.77 corrected for range restriction), showing predictive validity depends heavily on subgroup composition.
limitations: Single U.S. institution and a non-experimental correlational design; corrected correlations are sensitive to how subgroups are defined and to range restriction.
qualityRationale: Non-experimental correlational predictive-validity design at a single institution with no random assignment.

title: An Investigation of the Predictive Validity of the TOEFL iBT Test at an English-Medium University in Turkey
authors: O'Dwyer, J., Kantarcıoğlu, E., & Thomas, C.
design: Correlational predictive-validity study relating TOEFL iBT and an institutional proficiency exam to content/EAP course GPAs and instructor evaluations across two freshman semesters.
population: Undergraduate students, mainly Turkish nationals, at an English-medium institution in Turkey.
outcome: Correlations confirmed moderate to moderately high predictive validity of TOEFL iBT for content-course and English-course GPAs, particularly in technical fields; instructor evaluations showed fewer academic-English deficiencies for higher-scoring students.
limitations: Single-institution, correlational design; the report itself notes predictive validity research needs more comprehensive designs.
qualityRationale: Correlational, single-institution predictive-validity design without experimental manipulation.

title: Investigating the Predictive Validity of TOEFL iBT Test Scores and Their Use in Informing Policy in a United Kingdom University Setting
authors: Harsch, C., Ushioda, E., & Ladroue, C.
design: Mixed-methods study combining correlation/regression of TOEFL iBT scores against final academic award for a quantitative cohort with questionnaires/interviews from a qualitative subsample of students and tutors.
population: Postgraduate students entering a UK university (2011-2013) on the basis of TOEFL iBT scores, plus their EAP and academic tutors (48 students and 58 tutors in the qualitative strand).
outcome: Students entering on the basis of TOEFL iBT scores felt well prepared, regarded the test as effective preparation, coped well with linguistic demands, and a vast majority graduated successfully, underpinning the predictive validity of TOEFL iBT in a UK setting.
limitations: The qualitative subsample was self-selected, and the quantitative correlational/regression component cannot establish causation.
qualityRationale: Correlational/regression predictive-validity design plus a self-selected qualitative subsample; no experimental manipulation.

title: Recasts in the Adult English L2 Classroom: Characteristics, Explicitness, and Effectiveness
design: Classroom-based observational/correlational study coding naturally occurring teacher recasts across adult ESL classes, followed by a test of the relationship between recast characteristics and learner uptake/posttest accuracy.
population: 12 teachers and 118 adult ESL learners in intact classes ranging from 6 to 14 students, across 17 hours of meaning-based classroom interaction.
outcome: Recasts were widely used and were beneficial at least 50% of the time as measured by posttests. Stress, declarative intonation, one change, and multiple feedback moves predicted successful uptake, whereas interrogative intonation, shortened length, and one change predicted accuracy of test scores.
limitations: Single-country, classroom-observational design without a delayed retention measure, limiting causal claims about durable learning.
qualityRationale: Solid multi-classroom natural-data design with a reasonably large N, but correlational (non-experimental) and lacking a delayed posttest.

title: Uptake, Modified Output, and Learner Perceptions of Recasts: Learner Responses as Language Awareness
design: Experimental task-based interaction study in which learners received recasts on errors, then completed stimulated-recall sessions reviewing video of the recast episodes to probe perception of the feedback as corrective.
population: 24 learners of Japanese engaged in task-based interactions in which they received recasts of their errors.
outcome: In recast episodes where learners produced uptake, stimulated-recall reports indicated they perceived the recasts as corrective feedback significantly more frequently; in episodes where learners correctly repaired their errors, they were significantly more likely to report noticing the interlanguage-L2 mismatch.
limitations: Small sample (n=24) and single target language (Japanese) limit generalizability, and stimulated recall relies on retrospective self-report.
qualityRationale: Well-designed within-subject experimental link between uptake/repair and cognitive noticing, but small n and self-report outcome measure.

title: Peer Interaction and Corrective Feedback for Accuracy and Fluency Development: Monitoring, Practice, and Proceduralization
design: Quasi-experimental classroom study with four intact university English classes assigned to prompt-CF, recast-CF, peer-interaction-only, or control conditions over one semester of peer interaction training.
population: Four university-level English classes in Japan (N=167), each assigned to one of four treatment conditions.
outcome: The two corrective-feedback groups (prompts, recasts) improved in both overall accuracy and fluency (unpruned and pruned speech rates), whereas the peer-interaction-only group outperformed the control group only on fluency measures.
limitations: Treatment was delivered via peer-to-peer feedback training rather than expert/teacher feedback, and outcomes were measured only within one semester without long-term retention testing.
qualityRationale: Large classroom-based quasi-experiment (N=167) with random assignment of intact classes to four conditions and both accuracy and fluency outcome measures.

title: Effects of Form-Focused Practice and Feedback on Chinese EFL Learners' Acquisition of Regular and Irregular Past Tense Forms
design: Quasi-experimental study with three intact EFL classes randomly assigned to a prompt group, a recast group, or a content-only control group, completing form-focused production activities targeting English past-tense morphology.
population: 72 Chinese EFL learners at the university level in China.
outcome: Prompts had larger effects than recasts for increasing accuracy of regular (rule-based) past-tense forms, whereas prompts and recasts had similar effects on accuracy of irregular (exemplar-based) past-tense forms; the prompt group showed significant gains on all eight immediate/delayed posttest measures, the recast group on four, and the control group on three.
limitations: Single grammatical target (past tense) and single L1/instructional context (Chinese university EFL) limit generalizability to other forms or learner populations.
qualityRationale: Classroom quasi-experiment with random assignment of intact classes, a true control group, and multiple immediate/delayed outcome measures for two grammatical form types.

title: The Role of Procedural Learning Ability in Automatization of L2 Morphology under Different Learning Schedules: An Exploratory Study
design: Exploratory experimental study comparing automatization of L2 morphological rules for oral production under two spaced-practice schedules (short vs. long spacing), with procedural learning ability measured via the Tower of London task.
population: Sixty participants separated into two groups, studying morphological rules for oral production under short-spacing (3.3-day interval) and long-spacing (7-day interval) learning conditions.
outcome: Reaction time declined significantly in both groups after training, with the 3.3-day group showing a greater propensity for restructuring (measured by coefficient of variance) than the 7-day group; procedural learning ability was significantly associated with reaction time, but not with restructuring, in the 3.3-day group only.
limitations: Exploratory study, labeled as such by its own authors, with a moderate sample (N=60) split across two schedule conditions; automatization was assessed only via reaction-time/variability measures rather than long-term retention or free production.
qualityRationale: Explicitly labeled by its own authors as exploratory, with individual-differences analysis on a moderate sample, but methodologically rigorous spacing manipulation and cognitive-ability measure.

title: Massed Task Repetition Is a Double-Edged Sword for Fluency Development: An EFL Classroom Study
design: Quasi-experimental EFL classroom study in which learners repeated the same oral narrative task six times under massed, short-spaced, or long-spaced practice schedules; fluency was measured on immediate and one-week-delayed posttests using novel transfer stories.
population: 79 first-year Japanese university EFL students across four groups (massed n=20, short-spaced n=23, long-spaced n=21, control n=15; mean TOEIC score ~422).
outcome: Massed practice reduced breakdown fluency (pauses) the most on immediate posttests but produced slower articulation rate and more verbatim repetition; at the one-week delayed posttest, no significant differences among the three repetition schedules were found on most fluency measures.
limitations: Small sample size, especially the control group (n=15), with non-random assignment to conditions; individual cognitive differences were not controlled and analysis was limited to fluency, excluding complexity and accuracy.
qualityRationale: Well-designed classroom quasi-experiment with a clear multi-condition design, delayed posttest, and explicitly reported sample and limitations in a top SLA journal.

title: The Interaction Between Task Repetition and Oral Task Enjoyment: Effects on Speech Complexity, Accuracy, and Fluency
design: Classroom study examining how oral task enjoyment interacts with exact task repetition of a debate-style speaking task to affect L2 speech complexity, accuracy, and fluency measures.
population: 52 first-year English philology students (average age 19.56) at a Polish university, B2/Advanced-Mid proficiency.
institution: Stanisław Staszic University of Applied Sciences in Piła
outcome: Task repetition enhanced lexical diversity and marginally improved fluency; oral task enjoyment independently and positively influenced lexical diversity, correct verb forms, and speech rate; the interaction between enjoyment and repetition was not significant, suggesting repetition's benefits held regardless of enjoyment level.
limitations: Small sample size limiting generalizability, non-normal data distribution, single task type (debate) with a single coder, and lack of control for other individual differences such as motivation or anxiety.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed single-institution study with a modest sample and a non-significant interaction effect, but transparent methodology and stated limitations.

title: Negotiation of Meaning in Digital L2 Learning Interaction: Task Design Versus Task Performance
authors: Van der Zwaard, R., & Bannink, A.
design: Microanalytic study of native-speaker/non-native-speaker dyads completing a low-frequency-vocabulary negotiation task via both videoconferencing and text-based chat in a counterbalanced design, examining how task design shapes negotiated interaction.
population: Six NS-NNS dyads (N=12 participants) completing vocabulary negotiation tasks using videoconferencing and text-based real-time chat.
outcome: NNS responses shifted from task-appropriate to face-appropriate behavior over the course of interaction; NS interlocutors provided both face- and task-appropriate responses to secure task completion; prior misunderstandings shaped learners' expectations for subsequent negotiated items.
limitations: Very small sample (six dyads) limits generalizability; the qualitative microanalytic design trades statistical breadth for interactional depth.
qualityRationale: Rigorous microanalytic design in a top TESOL venue, but N of six dyads is very small.

title: Exploring Learner Perception and Use of Task-Based Interactional Feedback in FTF and CMC Modes
design: Stimulated-recall study comparing learners' noticing and subsequent use of interactional feedback during task-based interaction in face-to-face versus computer-mediated (synchronous text chat) modes.
population: 24 intermediate-level learners of Spanish as a foreign language.
outcome: Learners noticed feedback as feedback in both FTF and CMC modes, with no significant difference in perception accuracy between the two environments; however, differences emerged in learners' opportunities for and use of feedback depending on interaction mode and error type, contrary to predicted mode differences.
limitations: Small sample (n=24) limits statistical power; findings depend on stimulated recall, which relies on the accuracy of learners' self-reported noticing.
qualityRationale: Clear peer-reviewed method comparing interaction modes, but modest sample size and reliance on self-report via stimulated recall.

title: Comparing Traditional and Task-Based Approaches to Teaching Pragmatics: Task Design Processes and Learning Outcomes
authors: Kim, Y., Kang, S., D'Arienzo, M., & Taguchi, N.
design: Classroom intervention study comparing textbook-based (traditional) versus task-based (authentic blog-posting task) instruction of advice-giving pragmatic strategies among Korean EFL high schoolers, with immediate and 8-week-delayed posttests.
population: 50 Korean high school EFL students assigned to either traditional (textbook-based) or task-based (blog-posting) instruction conditions.
outcome: Both groups showed gains in advice-giving knowledge at immediate posttest, sustained at the 8-week delayed posttest; the task-based group demonstrated superior performance at immediate posttest, particularly for complex syntactic constructions used to mitigate advice.
limitations: Modest sample (n=50) split across two conditions; focuses on a single pragmatic feature (advice-giving) and a single L1/instructional context (Korean EFL high schoolers), limiting generalizability.
qualityRationale: Clear comparative classroom design with a delayed posttest, but a modest sample split across two conditions in a single context.
